The Record of Miraculous Responses to the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
Dharma Master Yan.
During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, there was a Dharma Master named Yan who resided at Zhaoti Temple in Chang’an; he became a monk at the age of eleven.
One day, he went with the monks of the temple to have his fortune told at the home of a physiognomist.

They took turns having their fortunes read, and when it was Yan’s turn, the physiognomist said, "It is a pity that one so intelligent shall meet an early end; at eighteen years of age, his lifespan will be exhausted. Hearing this, Yan was distressed.
Upon returning to the temple, he resolved to visit the sutra repository in person, where he burned incense, paid homage to the Triple Gem, and made a vow to practice.
He went to beg for a single scroll of scripture to uphold for the remainder of his life. Having finished his prayers, he reached into the scripture chest and drew out a scroll at random;
it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Thereupon, he devoted himself to its recitation and upholding, never ceasing day or night.
Suddenly one day, when the night had grown deep, he saw five-colored light within his room. In a brief moment, he saw a...

A Brahman monk, about one zhang and five chi in height, spoke to Yan, saying: "Your lifespan shall end at eighteen years; you will surely meet with an untimely death. Now, by the power of upholding and reciting Mahāyāna sūtras, your years have been extended. Having finished speaking, he vanished. Because of this verification, Yan became even more diligent in his practice. When he was over nineteen years old, he went out on a visit one day, and the physiognomist was struck with amazement. He said to Yan: [The rest of the passage follows: "How is it that your appearance has changed so much? You look as if you were a man of sixty or seventy! Your countenance is radiant and your complexion is clear. This is surely due to the merit of upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras. Yan replied, "I am indeed only nineteen years old. The physiognomist said, "If you had not upheld the Mahāyāna sūtras, you would have already died long ago. It is because of the power of the sūtras that your life has been prolonged. Yan then asked, "What is the merit of upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras? The physiognomist replied, "The merit of upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras is immeasurable. It can cause one to attain Buddhahood, or to become a Pratyekabuddha, or to become a Śrāvaka. It can also increase one's lifespan, eliminate calamities, and bring about all manner of blessings. How could I possibly describe it in full? Yan then prostrated himself in gratitude. From that time forward, he upheld the *Lotus Sūtra* with even greater devotion. At the age of twenty-four, he passed away peacefully while sitting in meditation. Later, when his body was cremated, a stupa was built for him. "I once remarked that your life would surely end prematurely," [the official] said. "I did not expect to meet you again today.

What wholesome deeds have you practiced that this sign of an early death has vanished and your dharma-life has been extended? Yan replied, "I have focused my mind exclusively on reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The physiognomist bowed his head and said, "We belong to the realm of worldly dust and do not understand the Buddha-dharma."
Such was the extraordinary excellence of his merit. When the Master went to visit Guan, the latter remarked that his lifespan would reach ninety-two years;
subsequently, this indeed accorded with the physiognomist's words, as he passed away at Zhaoti Temple (as recorded in the *Ganying ji*).
The Master Xun lived during the Sui dynasty in Wangli Village, to the west of Xinpan County in Yizhou. This lay practitioner, the Master Xun, concealed his traces and remained unassuming;
no one knew of him. Once, on an open space to the east of the village, he gazed far into the void and, with his own hand, wrote out the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Because he had transcribed the sutra, the various devas, nāgas, and spirits subsequently came to protect it. Whenever it rained, this area remained dry for about one *zhang*, as if covered by a roof.
Every time it rained, cowherds and young children would all take shelter there.
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a monk said to the villagers: "In the past, someone transcribed a sutra here, which resulted in [this phenomenon]."

The various devas established jeweled canopies above to provide protection; one must by no means allow people to tread upon them. Thereafter, railings were set up to encircle it as an offering to the Buddha image.
On every fast day, virtuous friends from near and far would gather to recite sutras and cultivate goodness.
One often heard the sound of celestial music, its resonance shaking the entire region, and thus it became a site of auspiciousness.
The śramaṇa Fazang was a person of the Sui dynasty. He resided at Baoshi Monastery in Fuzhou. By nature he was pure and ancient, and his religious practice was diligent and earnest.
Once, during the Kaihuang era, while constructing a monastery in Luozhou County of his native province, he took with him...
He sold his own robes and alms bowl to construct two halls and copied over eight hundred scrolls of scripture.

In the second month of the second year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, he suddenly fell ill. While in a state of deep sleep, he suddenly saw a Vajrapāṇi deity holding a scroll of scripture, who said to Fazang:
"In your construction of temples and copying of scriptures, there is the fault of 'interchanging' [resources]. I now..."
"I bestow upon you one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

If you can, with a sincere heart, copy this one fascicle of the sūtra and circulate it for reading and recitation, the sins of mutual exploitation shall all be completely extinguished. Having spoken these words, he vanished. Shortly thereafter, her illness was cured.

Thereafter, he sold all his clothing and possessions to copy one hundred fascicles of this sutra. He maintained it throughout his life, cultivating various virtuous deeds and avoiding worldly entanglements.

When he reached the age of ninety-nine, on the fifteenth day of the first month of that year, he invited the great assembly to read and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra) in seven fascicles and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The *Mìjīng* (Honey Sutra) consists of one volume and seven fascicles. He ascended the seat and sat upright; then, requesting a brush, he wrote a verse and bid farewell to the assembly. Suddenly, he passed away. Lu Yantong (Lu Baoyingji records him as Mu) was a man of the Sui dynasty.
He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten scrolls daily. When Li Mi’s rebellion broke out, Yantong was serving as a magistrate.

At Wulao, the local inhabitants wished to kill him in order to respond to the banner of righteousness. While there were rebels upon the city walls, they pursued and attempted to slay Yantong with swords.
Ahead lay a deep ravine; as the rebels drew near, he leaped into it.
In the air, he saw the Vajra deity, who pointed and commanded a person to catch Yantong’s arm and place him upon a rock. He suffered no injury at all. The divine being said, "You..."
Because he had maintained this sutra with such efficacy, a deity came specifically to rescue him; thus, he was able to remain safe and return home.
The arm upon which the spirit rested emitted a wondrous fragrance that did not dissipate for several days. Later, he rose to the rank of Fangbo (Regional Inspector).

At over eighty years of age, one day, without prior illness, he requested a brush to write a verse, bathed in fragrant water, and passed away while sitting upright. The verse said: "Eighty-nine years spent in this world."
Engaging in one’s livelihood as one goes along, today one lets go and proceeds; with bright moon and clear wind, one is free and at ease.

Chen Zhao (陳昭) lived during the Wude era of the Tang dynasty. The lay devotee Chen Zhao was a native of Jiangling. He regularly maintained a vegetarian diet and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

While he was accumulating meritorious practices through the study of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there was a large python that would come to the side of his seat daily to listen to the sutra, and depart as soon as it was finished.
This occurred every day. A neighbor named Li Chang, who was violent and lacked faith, saw the snake coming and going and suspected it was a malevolent spirit.
He lay in ambush and beat the snake to death. The snake, harboring a grievance, appealed to King Yama.
The King commanded his messengers to pursue Li Chāng’s soul to the underworld and have the snake coil around his body and bite him. The suffering was unbearable.

Li Chāng then appeared in a dream and told his wife, "During my lifetime, I killed a snake. Its original intent was to listen to one hundred scrolls of the sutras, by which it could have attained transcendence."
"Only seven fascicles remain. It was not right of me to have beaten him to death. Now that serpent’s suffering is beyond description;

you must request a monk for me to transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in seven fascicles, so that we may personally perform repentance before the Buddha to rescue it from its inverted and suspended calamity.
When his wife awoke, she recalled her dream and wished to follow through with the transcription of the scripture, but alas, their food supplies were insufficient. She redoubled...
His grief and suffering increased. He had a son named Saṃgharakṣita who was then five years old. When the boy asked his mother why she was weeping so bitterly, she told him the reason.
Saṃgharakṣita immediately replied to his mother, "Why do you not sell me away to save your father?

Thereupon, sobbing and choking with emotion, he took his child out to the market and sold him to a merchant from Shu for two strings of cash. As they were separated, his innermost being was wrung with pain.
In her deep anguish, she then requested a monk to transcribe seven fascicles of a sutra. Before the Triple Gem, she offered earnest prayers with a devoted heart, making two vows:
first, that her husband’s strength might flourish through the merit of the transcribed scripture and that their grievances might be resolved; second, that mother and son might once again be reunited.
Since their parting, she had remembered her son’s blindness and had done nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day while begging for alms in the marketplace. Her son—
He followed his traveling companion to Shu, from which he had not returned for thirty years. His adoptive parents had both passed away, and he suddenly thought of his biological mother;

he sold himself to write scriptures as an offering for his father’s posthumous merit, yet to this day he knows nothing of her survival or demise. He then gathered his household goods and returned to Jiangling to search for her.

Before he could see her, he purchased a house to dwell in temporarily. Suddenly, during the festival of the winter solstice when sacrifices were offered to the ancestors, he went to the vegetarian feast to beg for alms.
There were several elderly women. When they arrived, they recited one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and requested that the merit be dedicated for their benefit.
Saṃgharakṣita said, "I lost my father when I was young; my mother sold her own person to ransom me so she could offer sacrifices for his sake.

Now that I have managed to return to my hometown, I cannot find my mother. I pray that both my parents may together attain transcendence. Among them, an old woman suddenly cried out, "Young master! I am your mother!"
"You were five years old when you sold yourself to have a scripture copied for the memorial service of your father. I saw the contract for sale inside a basket at my residence.

When Saṃgharakṣita sought out the contract and read it, his grief and joy mingled together. He burned incense and prostrated himself before the Triple Gem, Heaven, Earth, and the deities, saying, "Now mother and son have met.
However, because my mother is blind, she cannot see her son. Thereupon, he took water and rinsed [her eyes].

He personally stood before Heaven and Earth and, together with his mother, licked her eyes; both sides were restored to sight, and thus the mother and son were reunited, fulfilling the prayers they had offered the previous year.
Among those who witnessed this, there was none who did not sigh with emotion.
Regarding Ren Wuniang:
In the first year of the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, at the quarters of the bhikṣuṇī at Jingde Temple in Luochuan, there was a female servant named Ren Wuniang.

After she had died, she requested to be enshrined as a spirit seat for offerings. After more than a month had passed, her younger brother and sister heard every night that the spirit seat possessed [a voice].
There was the sound of moaning. At first, [the master] was greatly terrified; he therefore burned incense and questioned it. The spirit immediately replied:
"In my life, I was unfit to commit five grave offenses: first, engaging in improper conduct within the chamber; second, having a fondness for eating beef; third, trampling upon the five grains;
fourth, pouring hot soup over [living things]; and fifth, killing sentient beings. Furthermore, I prepared minced raw fish as a delicacy. All those who were..."
"I killed sentient beings; they all reside in the Offices of the Shades and demand that I repay them one by one.

Now, in accordance with the decree of the Celestial Son Yama, I am made to undergo the hell of the Forest of Knives and the Trees of Swords. Day and night, I die ten thousand deaths and live ten thousand lives; the pain is unbearable.
At this very moment, there are seven knives upon my body, their agony penetrating to my very marrow. I address the ghost officials of the Netherworld with my own eyes:"

"What causes and conditions are there by which one may escape this suffering? The ghost official replied, "The evil karma you committed during your life was profound and heavy, and thus you have undergone this hell.

If you wish to be liberated from it, you must obtain filial descendants in the world of the living who can write out seven complete volumes of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Only then can you escape this suffering. He replied, "I have no other descendants; I have only my parents."
My younger brother and sister are at home. I beg you to grant me a brief respite from my suffering; I pray that you release me from this enclosure so that I may seek salvation.

Having received your permission, I shall return home. Relying on the affection between us as siblings, I hope that you will take the clothing and assets I left behind before my death, sell them to obtain money, and donate it to Jingtu Temple.
I request that Master Baoxian be commissioned to transcribe seven fascicles of scripture for me, and that I may personally perform repentance before the Buddha.
"Having committed various and boundless grave sins such as killing, I pray that I may soon be freed from the bitter suffering of hell.
Thereupon, her younger brother and sister followed her instructions and immediately sold her remaining possessions to commission monks to copy the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As soon as they had obtained one fascicle, the jailers of the underworld, acting upon an imperial decree, extracted [the karma] from Ren Wuniang’s body.
The knife. Having completed the transcription of seven fascicles of the sutra, the blade was entirely withdrawn.

By virtue of the merit of this Mahayana scripture, all sentient beings for whom she had sought retribution attained liberation. If they were born in the good realms, the karmic obstructions of Ren-er Niang were completely dissolved;
she emerged from hell and attained rebirth among humans and devas. One day she returned again to pay her respects to her younger brother and sister, just as she was about to—
Upon detailed inquiry, he was likewise nowhere to be seen (from the *Baoying ji*).
Bai Renzhe, during the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, served as the Magistrate of Zhuyang County in Guozhou. He was assigned to transport rice to Liaodong.

While crossing the sea, they were suddenly struck by a violent wind; looking in the four directions, all was dark and obscured. Renzhe and the eighty-two people on board were all filled with anxiety and fear.
However, as Renzhe had habitually recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his sincere devotion had moved the spirits.
At that moment, he composed his body and mind, burned incense, and began to read and recite the *Vajracchedikā*. Before the scroll was even finished, it was as if—
In a dream, he saw a Brahman monk in the sky whose body emitted five-colored light.
The monk said to Renzhe, "You and your company of over eighty people have karmic causes and conditions from past lives; today you shall all perish by drowning in the sea.

At this very moment, the various spirits, ghosts, and rākṣasas within the ocean are all watching for an opportunity to seize you. It is solely because of you, Renzhe," [that they have been restrained].

"By virtue of the merit of your daily recitation of the sutras, you have now received an edict from the Jade Emperor, which has been proclaimed throughout to the Dragon Kings and the deities of the water realms.
This shall ensure that you may avoid this calamity of sudden disaster. I have come specifically to inform you; do not harbor any anxiety or doubt.
In an instant, the wind subsided and the waves became calm, and all eighty-odd people were safely brought to shore. (From the *Baoying ji*).

In the first year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, Sima Qiaocheng served as the Director of the Court of Judicial Review (Dali Si). While on official duty, he encountered the mourning period for his mother; his grief was so profound that he became skeletal.

He drew blood to transcribe one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As soon as he had finished, three stalks of *zhicao* (fungus/herb) suddenly grew upon his mother’s tomb, reaching a considerable height.
One chi and eight cun in height, with green stems and crimson canopies; once taken, they would grow back again (*from the *Jingang ganying zhuan*).
During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, Wu Kui, a native of Yixing County in Changzhou, personally went to the Buddha [shrine] every day at the fifth watch.
Previously, he had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seventeen times while simultaneously performing prostrations and reciting the Buddha’s name.
He composed a poem that said: "The fifth watch bell tolls—do not indulge in sleep; Rouse your spirit and face the Buddha. One prostration, one invocation of Amitābha Buddha;
The lotus pond has already been planted with a single stem. Practice daily. At the age of ninety-two, he suddenly took leave of his children and grandchildren.
He passed away without illness. He saw two messengers leading him to an audience with King Yama. The King asked Kui, "What good deeds did you perform while alive?
Kui replied, "From my youth until now, I have focused my mind exclusively on reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. King Yama joined his palms and commanded Kui to sit.
As Kui recited the sūtra aloud, when he reached the passage concerning the city of Śrāvastī, a wondrous fragrance issued from his mouth, and he beheld the Buddha.
He manifested himself. The King was filled with incomparable joy and said to Kui, "You possess the merit of *prajñā*.

I shall issue an edict to send you to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, where you shall inherit the lineage of a high official, receive rank and emolument, enjoy wealth, honor, and blessings, and see your descendants flourish in glory.
Following these orders, the messenger escorted Kui back; as they passed his former home, he looked up into the air and addressed his children, saying, "I..."
By the power of the *Dharaṇī of Recollection*, King Yama has commanded me to be born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī; I have come specifically to bid you farewell.
You all should receive, uphold, and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The underworld authorities hold these two sūtras in profound reverence.

If you are unable to receive and uphold them, you should offer flowers and incense with respectful devotion; you will thereby obtain immeasurable merit. Furthermore, you must not take the lives of living beings.
"All wriggling and moving sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. By purchasing their lives and releasing them, one receives the retribution of longevity.
When his children heard this, they wept bitterly and said, "Do not be so distressed. When a person is born into this world, there is at least one good deed upon which to rely.

When life ends, it is like sleeping through the night and waking at dawn; one will again see the sun and moon. If one has consistently dwelled in evil, one will surely enter the darkness. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
[Recorded in the *Zazuzuji*].

During the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, a horse-thief falsely accused a filial and incorrupt official (*xiaolian*) of being an accomplice. He was subjected to torture for ten days, yet [the official] did not [confess].

He suffered severe physical torment, yet there was no incriminating testimony. The investigating officials suspected it was a wrongful case, and no formal record had been finalized. The Xiao-lian (Xiao Lian) devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
his voice was mournful and piercing, continuing day and night without ceasing. Suddenly, one day, a section of bamboo appeared.
The two halves had joints where they met; having fallen upon the ground, no one knew from whence they had come. The prisoners all vied with one another to seize and examine them.
They were carried before the jailer, who, suspecting that knives might be hidden within, split them open before the assembly.

Upon inspection, there was found a half-verse from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* which said: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas. The multitude all arose in astonishment.
Respectfully. The leader of the bandits repented his transgressions and was consequently released.
Zhou Boyu, during the eleventh year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, served as the Vice Governor of Weizhou; he regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he never altered his resolve whether in public or private, making it his daily practice.
One day, he suddenly saw a monk from India appear before him. Boyu asked, "Who is this venerable one? He replied, "I am Subhūti from the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
I have been reciting the sutra for you for several years; it is a pity that you do not cease eating meat. If you were to set your heart upon it with sincerity..."
Those who seek the Buddha-way must observe the long fast and abstain from meat. From this time forth, Boyu ceased eating meat and subsisted on vegetarian food;
he increased his diligent practice, reciting and upholding the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra without ceasing, regardless of cold or heat. (From the *Zhengyan Fu*).

The Preface to the *Recorded Miracles of Chan Master Wang Daizhi* states: In the past, during the Tang dynasty, there was an official of the Imperial Secretariat named Wang Daizhi. While traveling by boat upon the Han River, he was detained by the wind;
the waves surged violently, and all four directions were shrouded in darkness. The masts snapped and the oars broke, leaving him in extreme peril. The entire crew was struck with terror.
Our lives were not to be spared, and I, the Waizhi, was also filled with dread.

Having no other recourse, I took the single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that I had habitually recited throughout my life and cast it into the river; immediately, the wind and waves became calm.

Since then, the Waizhi has remembered this sutra more deeply than ever. Having upheld it for many years, he remained heavy-hearted and unhappy. After traveling for two months, he finally arrived at Zhenjiang and saw...
About a hundred paces from the stern of the boat, there was an object resembling a ball, appearing and disappearing at no fixed time. The assembly suspected it was something extraordinary.
The Waidai (Director of the Imperial Library) dispatched men to call for fishermen to retrieve it; it turned out to be a cluster of snails rolled into a single mass.

When they cut it open, the exterior was moist while the interior was dry. The Waidai used his hand to separate them and examined them; they were none other than the sutras he had cast away the previous day, down to the finest detail.
There was no harm. The Attendant-in-Waiting was filled with wonder and joy; he bowed and accepted it, sighing in admiration:
"The Han River meets the Nine Bays and flows as far as Nanxu, covering many thousands of li. The boats and vessels coming and going there are beyond counting.
Yet I have never heard of a scripture being carried from that place to this one. That a common snail saw it and would not let go—was it for its fame? Its profit? Or its wealth?"
Is it not the case that those who seek liberation from the cycle of birth and death must surely do so? Alas! Among all things, only humans are most sentient.
There are those who throughout their entire lives never hear this sutra; there are those who hear it but do not see it; there are those who see it but do not believe it;

and there are those who believe it yet, for the sake of fame, profit, wealth, and sensual form, allow their minds to be enslaved by these things and are unable to uphold it. Such persons are not even equal to a snail.

This is called the most spiritual; who could rival it? Written on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month in the seventh year of the Shaoxi era of the Song dynasty, the year being Dinghai, by the recluse Xiaozi.
I reverently record that during the Qiannian era of the Tang dynasty, the monk Qianhui of Guangzhou had been upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since childhood,
never wavering through cold or heat. He was then traveling by sea with several dozen monastics and laypeople toward the Nan’an Protectorate when he suddenly encountered a storm.
A great surge arose, wrecking the vessels. All those on board perished in the sea, except for Qianhui, who happened upon a thicket of mugwort amidst the waves.
He gradually climbed onto the mugwort, remaining there with the tide for three days and three nights.
Only then did he reach the shore. Looking closely into the reeds, he saw a single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which was not at all damp or wet.
With devout reverence, he received this scripture, making offerings to it with utmost sincerity and upholding it day and night.

When he reached the age of one hundred and thirty, he sat upright and passed away. From the very source where the scripture had emerged, incense smoke gradually formed five-colored clouds that slowly [disappeared].
It ascended to the celestial realms. The assembly of virtuous monks, high-ranking officials, and the clergy and laity from near and far all halted at this spot, awaiting the descent of the scripture.
After one day and one night had passed, they knew not where it had gone.

Lady Sinu was the daughter of Duke Sinu of the Tang state of Chen. She was the younger sister of Lu Shiren, Duke Rui of Kuan. In her daily life, she delighted in doing good and believed in the retribution of sin and merit.
She used to recite the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; when two or three sections remained until the end of the scroll, she suddenly suffered from a severe headache.

As she was writing, she thought to herself, "If I were to die, I would not be able to finish this scroll. She summoned all her strength despite her illness to seek out a candle, determined to complete it to its full end.

However, the flames were suddenly extinguished, and her maidservant returned empty-handed. The lady sighed incessantly. Suddenly, she saw a lamp and torch gradually ascend into the hall and enter directly into her bedchamber;
though there was no one to hold it and it was three feet above the ground, its radiance was like that of day. The lady was struck with amazement.
Hsi was startled and hurriedly took up the scripture to read it. After a short while, her family members struck flint to produce fire, and the light of the candle immediately went out.
From then on, her illness also healed. She recited five scrolls daily. One day, when Master Rui was about to die, his wife went to visit him.

The Master said to his wife, "My younger sister recites the scriptures with such devotion that the records of the underworld have noted her name, and her lifespan has been extended. It was extraordinary.
On that day, there was surely a favorable karmic retribution. When the Master’s life reached ninety years, he was free from illness;
he requested a bath, sat upright, and passed away. —The Monk Sandao.
During the Tang Dynasty, Cui Zhao served as the Prefect of Shouzhou. There was a strong man who had committed a crime punishable by the ultimate penalty.
At the moment of execution, an official was dispatched to escort him to the marketplace for decapitation. When three successive blows of the blade were struck, each sword broke on its own.

The Prefect asked the strong man, "What artifice do you possess? He replied, "I have no other artifice; I have simply devoted myself throughout my life to the recitation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*."
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he then dispatched someone to fetch the scripture for inspection.

Upon opening the case and looking at it, he saw that the text had already been divided into three sections, with the seams clearly visible. When the Prefect saw this, he joined his palms in joy and praised it, saying:
"I have often heard that this sūtra possesses inconceivable merit; now it truly is so. He subsequently commuted the soldier's sentence. The soldier—
He sought to leave the household life and become a monk; the Provincial Governor immediately granted him a *duodie* (ordination certificate). He was styled the "Three-Swords" (*Sandao*) Master.
Qian Xingli of Shanzhou was illiterate; during the early years of the Changqing era, he constantly followed a virtuous friend who orally transmitted the teachings to him.

After one year, he was able to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from memory. Whenever he traveled about in his ordinary body, he would carry a copy of the scripture with him, burning incense and chanting it;
he would complete one fascicle in a single day. Once, he happened to purchase over three hundred strings of silk cloth to sell in other prefectures.
As he was crossing a steep mountain pass, he encountered several bandits, each of whom was armed with a blade.

They came rushing to catch him as he stood there. His chest and boxes weighed approximately fifty catties; he hurriedly cast them away and fled to take cover beside a deep ravine at the foot of a ridge.
Suddenly, he saw a Vajrapāṇi deity in the air pointing its finger toward where he stood;

he felt as though his body were upon the surface of the water, walking as if on level ground. When the bandits saw the chests and bundles, they immediately seized them, but when they lifted them, they found them exceedingly heavy.
He was unable to rise. The bandits were all struck with wonder. Remaining on the ridge, he beckoned with his hand and called out to Xingli, saying, "Come up the ridge!
If I were to kill you, it would be as if I were killing my own parents. Xingli immediately climbed up.

The bandits questioned him repeatedly, asking, "What illusory arts do you possess? He replied, "I possess no illusory arts; it is likely that I have merely been single-mindedly reciting [mantras] in my daily life."
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* manifested such a miraculous wonder through the spiritual resonance of the Buddha’s power.
Consequently, the bandits ordered Xingli to open the case and examine it; he then beheld five-colored radiance appearing upon it.
All the bandits joined their palms in repentance and surrendered one hundred strings of cash to Xingli, who took the scripture and departed to receive and uphold it. The multitude likewise...
He made a vow to abandon his spear and sword and never commit robbery again; thus they all reformed their evil ways and followed the good (as recorded in the *Ganying zhuan*).
Regarding Lingyou:
Lingyou was a monk who left the household life at Daxingshan Temple in the capital. In the second year of the Changqing era, he died suddenly after having been deceased for seven days.

The following day, his body felt slightly warm, yet it had not yet been encoffined. He saw two messengers lead him before King Yama, who questioned him regarding the deeds he had practiced while in the world of the living.
The deceased replied, "I, a poor monk, throughout my life constantly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King joined his palms, granted him a seat, and commanded him to recite it aloud once. [At that moment, the torments of hell ceased. The boiling and beating of the hells...
The suffering of Chu was temporarily relieved. When the recitation of the sutra was finished, the Son of Heaven asked You again, "In this recited scripture, there is one chapter missing.
Your master’s allotted lifespan has reached its end; I now add ten years to your life. Upon returning to the world, you must exhort others to receive and uphold this sutra.
The authentic copy is at Zhongli Temple in Haozhou, inscribed upon a stone stele. Once You had returned to his soul, he recorded the details in a memorial.
He reported this to the Tang Emperor. By imperial decree, an imperial messenger was dispatched to the stele in Haozhou to examine this chapter.
It states: "There is no dharma that can be taught; this is called teaching the Dharma. This refers to what was later added:
at that time, Subhūti addressed the Tathāgata, saying, "Non-sentient beings are called 'sentient beings. This is it.

Shi Mingjun died suddenly during the first year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. Upon reviving, he said that he had seen two people dressed in green robes lead him before the King of the Netherworld.

The King asked, "What karma did you perform throughout your life? Mingjun replied, "I did nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King said, "Excellent! If you have recited it ten times..."

"Recite ten thousand times; next year you will surely be born in the Pure Land, and as a disciple, you shall not see me again. He then released him to return home. From that time on, Sengjun redoubled his diligent practice.
In the third month of the second year, he passed away. The entire community of monks at the monastery all smelled a wondrous fragrance. (From the *Benzhuan*.)
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Su Renqin in Chang’an. His father, in a previous life, had borrowed "rebirth money" from the underworld;
having obtained a place of rebirth, he enjoyed wealth, nobility, and blessings throughout his worldly life. Consequently, he never repaid the debt. After he died, [the account remained unsettled].
Thereafter, he fell into a latrine, where he was burdened by sand and stones; submerged in foul filth, he endured immeasurable suffering.
Furthermore, while Renqin was alive, he relied upon his wealth and status, lacking any sense of shame or remorse; he slaughtered pigs and sheep at will, roasting and boiling living beings.
This is because the sentient beings who were killed have each filed complaints before the various courts of the underworld.
Furthermore, the spirits of both the hidden and the manifest have recorded their transgressions, leading to their being summoned and registered by the offices of the netherworld.

Your benevolent and honorable soul has been detained in prison, causing you to suffer from various grave illnesses in this world, lying bedridden for years without recovery. Due to these evil karmic actions of killing, your allotted lifespan has been diminished.

He died prematurely. He saw two messengers who escorted him to appear before King Yama. The King commanded, saying: "Because you cultivated merit in your previous life, you attained wealth and abundance in this present life.
Now, you have indulged yourself in enjoying these blessings and failed to recognize the law of cause and effect, resulting in your slaughter of sentient beings."

Consequently, his lifespan was reduced and his stipend cut off; he was driven by the wardens of hell onto the peaks of the Knife Mountain and the Sword Trees to undergo retribution for his various evils.
Thereupon, filled with panic and terror, he looked up and addressed the King, saying: "Think of me with benevolence!

Although I did not study the scriptures or perform good deeds during my life, I once gave wealth to request the redemption of one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which I then donated to the monks of Anguo Temple."
The monk Shenjing received and upheld it with reverence. After this monk passed away, could there not be a karmic response?

In a brief moment, a wondrous fragrance wafted forth, and the monk Shenjing was seen holding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in his hand, proceeding directly to the presence of the Heavenly Son’s palace.

He said, "I, a poor monk, have long been honored by Your Majesty for receiving and upholding this sūtra, thereby achieving the merit of Prajñā. For this reason, I have come specifically to inform the King; I pray that [you continue to uphold it]."
"Bestow your compassion! Grant Renqing his life back once more so that he may reform his evil ways and follow the good.

The King then joined his palms and decreed that Renqing’s lifespan be extended by fifty years, and he returned to the world of the living. Because he had regained his life, those among the neighbors, both near and far, who saw or heard of it—
All were filled with awe and admiration; each vowed to abstain from killing and turned their hearts toward the good. Renqin was restored to life.

He then resolved to print one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and one thousand scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, provide a vegetarian feast for one hundred monks, and perform the Great Water and Land Offering (*shuilu daizhai*) along with various other meritorious deeds.
Suddenly, one night he dreamed of his deceased father, who said: "I have been suffering the torments of hell without end..."
"Thank you for your practice of the Buddha-dharma. By the power of that merit, I have already attained rebirth in the heavenly realms.
If you were to take one hundred mu of my fields and dedicate them to the temple to provide offerings for the Buddha and meals for the monks, this merit would be inconceivable;

it would transcend the seven generations of ancestors and its blessings would extend to your descendants. Renqin then followed his deceased father’s instructions, thereby fulfilling his heart's wish. (From...)
(From the *Jazuzhiji*):
During the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Yang Xun served as the Judicial Commissioner of Kuizhou. He constantly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, maintaining a correct state of mind.
Zhi accumulated hidden merits (*yin-gong*) that moved the heavens above. His son was twenty-three years old and was studying for the civil service examinations.
One day, he informed his father that he wished to enter the examination hall. His father said, "Your learning is not yet sufficient; you must not go.

That night, his father dreamed of a Vajrapāṇi deity who said to him: "Because of your recitation of sutras and your hidden merits, there has been a response. I have come specifically to report this to you."
"Your son will surely become noble in the future. If he is to succeed in the imperial examinations, you must change his name to Yang Chun (楊椿) and submit his application under that name;
I shall assist him with my pen during the examination hall. After ten days, he received this dream. The following day, he had his son compose the examination essay under the name Yang Chun.
Indeed, he achieved sixth place. The following year, when he went to take the provincial examination, Yang Chun himself dreamed of a Vajra deity who spoke to him...
Chun said, "This year’s examination theme concerns 'ruling as a king by practicing the Way of Kings. You must prepare your mind in advance; do not let this leak out at all.
On the day of the actual examination, it was exactly as he had dreamed. Chun ranked ninety-sixth.
When the palace examination concluded, the examiners placed three scrolls upon the imperial dais. After selecting an auspicious day to open the seals and call the names, Chun appeared once more.
Again, he dreamed that a deity spoke to him, saying: "Your composition is excellent; however, it does not accord with the examiner's intent and has been placed in the fifth rank.
I shall now exchange your scroll for the first-place scroll upon the Imperial Throne. When the names are called on a later day, [you shall be the first]."
"You ought to seize the position of the Grand Marshal of the realm. Because of the merit of you and your father’s lifelong recitation of sutras and practice of goodness, it has come to this;

the fruit truly accords with your dream. When Shi Yan heard that Yang Xunzi had been promoted to Grand Marshal of the realm, he invited Xun to take his seat and requested that Xun be relieved of his duties.
Xun told Lord Shi: "I have always looked up to and relied upon Your Honor as my second heaven."
Under his protection, I have served the public for forty years. My family possesses no assets; I have accumulated only hidden merit (yin-de), which has resulted in three bags of coins.
I beg for Your Majesty’s permission to bring them forth and open them before the court. The first bag contains thirty-nine wen, equivalent to three qian.
The second bag contains over four thousand wen of half-denomination coins. The third bag amounts to ten thousand small coins.

The Magistrate did not know why. Xun said, "Every year when I preside over judicial investigations, whenever there is a prisoner facing the death penalty, I examine their circumstances and, if they may be spared, I determine a sentence of exile.
I then cast a coin worth three *dang*. If it lands on the side for those who have committed an offense punishable by exile—"

He was sentenced to the crime of *tu* (corvée labor). He threw down one *ch'e-erh* coin. For those who committed offenses punishable by the *zhàng* (staff) punishment, he would measure the severity of the case and sometimes release them;
for these, he would simply throw down one small coin. Furthermore, following the example of Zhou Chi, he practiced the ten kinds of benefits of the *Taishang Ganying Pian*.

First, he collected abandoned infants from the streets and markets, hiring others to care for and raise them, and waited until they were old enough to be returned to their families so that they might recognize him.
First, they shall be reunited with their parents in a joyful gathering.

Second, beginning from the third day of the eleventh month each winter, those aged sixty and above and those under fifteen who are beggars shall be taken into the family’s charitable almshouse. Each person shall be provided daily with one *sheng* of rice and fifteen cash.
By the third day of the second month, having completed one quarter of the year, they shall be permitted to go as they please.

1. Seeking to provide for [the needy]. 2. Widely distributing efficacious medicinal decoctions to relieve the suffering of those afflicted by disease. 3. Providing coffins for families who are destitute and unable to afford the funeral transport of their kin.
4. When there are female servants who are no longer fit for service, one shall not calculate their price;

instead, providing them with clothing and funds, they may remarry as they see fit. 5. Throughout one’s life, one shall single-mindedly refrain from killing and protect all sentient beings. Whenever one encounters...
7. To purchase and redeem the lives of flying and running creatures and release them. 8.

Whenever encountering years of famine and scarcity, to buy grain at high prices and sell it at low prices to provide relief for the poor. 9. To repair any temples or monasteries that have collapsed or suffered damage;
to refurbish sacred images that have become weathered and peeling over time; and to restore bridges, roads, and irrigation channels that have fallen into disuse. All...

9. For those who govern, there may be gentlemen from distant districts or travelers who have become wayward and lost. One should measure the distance traveled and provide them with provisions for their journey, enabling them to return safely to their own regions.
10. I, Xun, am humbled by my appointment as an investigating magistrate. Whenever I encounter a prisoner condemned to death, I grant them a reprieve to return to life.

I constantly apply the principle of "extending oneself to others" to relieve the urgent needs of others and rescue them from peril. My sincerity has moved the High Heavens, and they have granted me [this] favor.
That I, a man, have today won the title of Grand Champion of the realm is entirely due to the merit of serving the public and practicing virtue throughout my life.
How could I dare abandon the gates of officialdom to retire and seek personal ease? I have two poems to present to the Magistrate.
The poems say: [Poem 1] [Poem 2]
Yang Chun of Kui Prefecture became the provincial examination head (Zhuangyuan) and served as a civil official for forty years;
by showing compassion and sparing countless lives, he accumulated meritorious deeds that moved Heaven.
People say, "The gates of officialdom are not to be entered," but I say, "The gates of officialdom are good places for cultivation, provided one does not allow right and wrong to become inverted."
With inverted feet, she treads upon lotus flowers, giving birth at every step.
Hezhen’s daughter, Hezhen’s wife Lady Liu,
was twenty-six years of age when she gave birth to a son who had reached two weeks of age, and a daughter who had reached one week.
Faman suddenly dreamed one night that she had entered the underworld, where it was decreed that Lady Liu’s life would end in the third month of the following spring.

Upon waking, she brooded over this and wept incessantly in grief and alarm. Her husband and relatives all asked her the reason for her lamentation, and she replied: [The remainder of the text follows.]

Once, I dreamed that I entered the Office of the Underworld, where it was decreed that I had only half a year remaining in this world. When the time arrived, I died exactly as predicted and felt no regret;

however, I was grieved that my children and grandchildren would be left without support. Suddenly, one day, I reflected upon myself and immediately commissioned an artist to paint a scroll depicting Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
I reverently made offerings to it, renounced meat and wine, and from morning until night personally stood before the Buddha, practicing with utmost diligence.
Reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he made this dedication and vow: "I pray only that through the compassionate grace of the Buddha, my life may be prolonged.
If I reach forty-five years of age, may my children all have reached the time for marriage; even when I die and enter the Yellow Springs, I shall be at peace.
Daily I shall recite with single-minded devotion until I reach thirty-eight years of age, at which time my son shall have taken a wife."
When she reached the age of forty-three, her daughter was married, thereby fulfilling her wish.

In the winter of the fourth year of the Taihe era, having just completed her forty-fifth year, she gave away all her clothing and assets to adorn a Buddha image; thus, her virtuous deeds were fully accomplished.
One day, she informed all her kinsmen and relatives: "The time of my death has arrived. Why do you worry? It is because I am possessed by a malevolent spirit."
She did not believe this was possible. On New Year’s Day, Lady Liu personally invited a virtuous *śramaṇa* to receive the Eight Precepts of the Fast before the Three Jewels.

Having bathed and changed her clothes, she sat alone in a single room in the *paryaṅka* posture, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in a loud voice. Upon finishing the recitation, she became silent and still.
Her children, grandchildren, and relatives all entered the room to look upon her; she sat upright and had already passed away, yet she appeared as if alive, with a solemn and radiant countenance.

Only the crown of her head was warm, burning to the touch. Among the fourfold assembly of monastics and the common people, there were none who, upon seeing or hearing of this, did not take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem, praising it as a rare wonder.
Her husband, deeply grieved, followed the funeral rites for a deceased monk and constructed a stupa for her.
He was buried at the northern city wall of Jing (from the *Youyang zazu*).
During the Qianfu era of the Tang dynasty, there was a military officer; the Prefectural Governor of Yanzhou, Minister Cui, was extremely strict in his laws and regulations. There was one soldier...
The military officer failed to attend the morning court audience. Lord Cui was greatly incensed and ordered his attendants to execute him.
As the officer was being put to death, his countenance remained entirely unchanged. The crowd marveled at this. Once the execution was completed, the officer woke from his sleep at the third watch.
Seeing only his body lying on the street, he hurried home. His wife and children were all struck with terror, fearing it was a ghostly apparition.
He said to his wife and children, "I am no ghost. When I was first beheaded, I was as if in a drunken dream and knew nothing of what was happening.
Now I have suddenly awakened and returned. The whole family rejoiced. The next morning, he went before the tent and bowed in thanks to Lord Cui.
Startled, he asked, “What art do you possess that you dare come here again? The military officer replied, “I have never possessed any other art.
From my youth until now, I have daily recited three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Yesterday morning, before dawn, I exceeded the allotted time for my recitation and thereby violated military discipline. Cui asked again, “Did you know when you were to be executed? He replied, “When I was first led out.”
Outside the gate, he felt as though his body were in a drunken dream; he could remember nothing at all. He asked again, "Where is the scripture you were reciting?
He replied, "It is inside a case in the Buddha-chamber at home. Cui urgently ordered it to be brought out.
When the case was opened, only five-colored rays of light were seen. Upon taking the scripture to examine it, it had already been split into two pieces. Cui was greatly alarmed.
He was deeply remorseful and personally repented his transgressions. He consoled his military officers, saying, "I shall provide you with silk and cloth;
you may purchase silver foil to copy one hundred scrolls of this sutra. At Yan-shou Temple, I will command the monks to chant and recite it as an act of repentance.

He then distributed all the funds at once, reserving ten scrolls to be reverently enshrined for worship in the Buddha Hall of his own temple. Furthermore, he ordered that the execution scene be depicted in painting.
At that location, he also cut down an image of the sutra to manifest its miraculous traces (from the *Baoying ji*).
During the Zhenghe era of the Tang dynasty, there was a stone mason named Old Man Sun from Zhenzhou who daily recited three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
One day, he entered the mountains with more than thirty others to quarry stone when the mountain suddenly collapsed.

They were all lost within it, yet Master Sun alone survived, having been caught in a fissure in the rock. After twelve years had passed, his descendants were quarrying the stone again until they pierced through to where their grandfather sat upright, his appearance unchanged from before.
His descendants bowed in astonishment and asked how he had managed to survive. The old man replied: "I constantly..."

He was reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [The old man] asked again, "Are you hungry? He replied, "At the very beginning, because I ate a single piece of *sarpis* cake, I have not been hungry until now.
The old man asked, "Is the sūtra I used to study still here? His descendants answered, "It is. Thereupon, he returned home.
He reached out from afar to take up the scripture and examine it; upon it was a circular hole, exactly the size of a butter cake.

All who saw or heard of this could not help but praise the scripture for its inconceivable merit, noting that it had been able to rescue the old man Sun from the peril of starvation and death by thirst. (From the *Baoying ji*).
In the past, there was County Magistrate Liu of Mount Bi. He served as an official with integrity and maintained a very strict family code.

Every day he recited three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, never ceasing regardless of cold or heat. While serving previously as a staff member of the Provincial Administration Commission, his wife was in her seventh month of pregnancy and dreamed of a monk.

Coming from the void, he said: "I have a matter to trouble your venerable hearing. This poor monk has practiced for over sixty years, yet because worldly conditions were not yet exhausted, I was compelled to reappear in this world.
Perceiving that your roots of goodness have reached maturity, I have come specifically to seek refuge under you."
"Please accept me. Liu replied, "Since you have been so graciously spared, do not be sparing with your instruction. The monk then entered the bedroom. Liu woke up in anger.
The next day, his wife gave birth to a daughter who was exceptionally intelligent and surpassing others. When she was seven years old—
Without ever having studied under a teacher, she mastered all the scriptures. Following her father’s example, she recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily;
in less than a month, she was able to recite it from memory. Her parents were greatly pleased. When she reached the age of nineteen, she composed verses with poetic grace.
Once, after recovering from an illness during the summer months, she suddenly wrote a poem about mosquitoes, saying: "Yesterday we had no appointment with you, yet this morning..."
"Entering the gauze curtains of my own accord, I let you feast upon my jade-like body; even after a full meal, I still make coquettish sounds—on whom else am I so dependent?
Her father heard this and was greatly incensed. He summoned her before the hall and severely rebuked her for her audacity, intending to place her in a position of death.
Her mother hurried to her rescue and inquired into the circumstances. The daughter said, "Last night mosquitoes bit me; today I composed this poem. There is nothing else to it."

Regarding another matter, the mother immediately went to inform the father, explaining the circumstances. The father said, "Since you are still a maiden in your chamber, how could you speak such words?
Every sentence contains deep meaning. The daughter told her father, "Not so; please grant me the title, and I shall compose four lines myself."
The father took up a pair of scissors as his prompt; the daughter replied offhand:

"When sentient beings join their two thighs, when insentient things open their two thighs—quickly take them from your waist and cut them to length as you please. The father smiled slightly and remained silent.
The daughter then entered her room, sought a bath, changed her clothes, and came out to the hall to address her father: "Nian-nu was nearly deprived of her life just now. Not so.
As if having bid farewell to one's parents early in the morning, he composed this verse: "For nineteen years I have been a guest in purity;
Without flowers or indulgence, it is clear and distinct. Returning, I leave it to the east, west, south, or north;
Life is finished, death is finished— Regardless of whether one is old or young. Today, having turned the pivot, I encounter the True Void; A single wheel."
The bright moon is pure and radiant; it is difficult to depict and difficult to paint. With flowers adorning his head, he sits cross-legged, passing into nirvana.
By Song Chengxin.

In the second year of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, there was a man named Song Chengxin who lived in Huating County, Xiuzhou. He suffered from the ailment of reversed stomach (upward vomiting) for several years, yet none of the hundred medicines could cure it. One night, he suddenly dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to Chengxin: "It is because of the enmity and transgressions of your past lives that you have come to suffer these various illnesses in this present life. Do you understand? Chengxin replied: "I do not know. The monk continued: "If you wish to eliminate your karmic obstacles, you must recite the name of the Buddha Amitābha ten thousand times each day. Once you have completed one hundred thousand recitations, you will see me again. Chengxin woke up and immediately began to recite the Buddha’s name. After three days, he dreamed of the same monk, who told him: "Your karmic obstacles have been extinguished; you shall soon be free from illness. Chengxin subsequently recovered his health. Later, when he was about to die, he saw the monk once more, who led him away. Chengxin passed away peacefully. His son, Song Zhi, recorded this account. It is preserved in the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), fascicle 47. It is also recorded in the *Shishi Jigu Lue* (Brief Account of Past and Present Buddhist Affairs), fascicle 10. Furthermore, the *Xinxiu Fozu Tongji* (Newly Revised General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), fascicle 50, records that Chengxin was originally a Daoist priest who had converted to Buddhism. He died at the age of eighty-four. The aforementioned accounts differ slightly in their details. As for the efficacy of the Buddha’s name, it is as vast as the ocean; how could it be limited to only one hundred thousand recitations? This is merely an example of a specific case where the response was swift due to the gravity of the karmic obstruction. Therefore, those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land should not be negligent in their practice. One must constantly maintain mindfulness of the Buddha and diligently cultivate the path. Only then can one hope to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. How could it be otherwise? Thus, it is said: "The power of the Buddha’s name is like the great ocean; its benefits are immeasurable. Even if one were to recite it for ten thousand kalpas, the merit would never be exhausted. One should take this as a warning and apply it to oneself. How could one possibly fail to believe it? This is the twenty-seventh story. It is also recorded in the *Jingtu Shengxian Lu* (Record of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land), fascicle 2. Furthermore, the *Wangsheng Xifang Jingtujing Zhuanji* (Collection of Biographies of the Scripture on Rebirth in the Western Pure Land), fascicle 3, records that Chengxin was originally a Daoist priest who later became a Buddhist layman. He died at the age of seventy-nine. The aforementioned accounts differ slightly in their details.
